The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00506

Proving that the world depends on no creatorless force, but on a Maker who brings things into existence without being changed by them or made a subject for them, is one of the most important questions in philosophy. Whoever fails to understand God's oneness in action will not understand His oneness in being, His necessary existence, His power, knowledge, will, wisdom, or any of His other attributes. Once a person understands this question, and understands the soul, its survival, and its return after death, after learning its origin, maker, and oneness, that person has gained a great deal of knowledge. The remaining questions matter less.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00507

When this question is settled, and we understand the causes of new events and the passing away of things, and how bodies and their natures are renewed from moment to moment—as scripture and reason both indicate, without undermining sound philosophy—we have laid the clearest and firmest path toward intellectual unveiling and direct insight. People are puzzled by how the Necessary Being, who never changes, can bring about new events without taking on a new feature. Until a person is certain about this question and related ones, inquiry cannot rest on a firm foundation. If God could act in an arbitrary way, without reasons, there would be no meaningful account to give and no rational order to discover.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00508

One of the mystics says: “To say that the world is eternal in time is empty talk. Ask what is meant by the world. If it means all bodies, such as the heavens and the elements, or everything besides God, then the statement is still wrong. In the second sense, many things included in the world do not depend on time for their existence. In the first sense, it would mean that bodies have existed for as long as time has existed, implying that time existed before bodies. But bodies exist before time, at least in the order of nature. If the speaker means neither of these, we cannot know what he means. We have answered what we understood; arguing about what we do not understand is for the blind.”
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00509

He continues: “If someone means that bodies have existed for as long as God has existed, that is a grave error. Bodies do not exist where God exists—not now, before, or after. Anyone who says the world exists now alongside God is also gravely mistaken. Where God is, in the oneness of His being, there is no time or place. Yet no time, place, or particle of the world is without Him. He is with every particle, but nothing possible is with Him. His existence precedes the world's, just as it precedes the written form of the words on this page, with no difference between the two. Whoever thinks there is a difference is still caught in doubt and has not freed God from time, any more than ordinary people free Him from place when they imagine Him as a body. Such a person is far from the true faith that a mystic grasps at the beginning of the spiritual path: God is prior to the future just as He is prior to the past. This is certain to the mystic, though many scholars cannot understand it.”
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00510

I say: this mystic's account does not settle the question of whether the world began. Those who say that the heavenly bodies and the basic elements have always existed agree that God relates to the future as He does to the past. They are not unable to understand that bodies do not exist where the First Reality exists, whether now, before, or after. Every effect is like this in relation to its source. Even so, they say that the heavens and other things last forever.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00511

They can explain the world's eternity by saying that bodies are not preceded by a stretch of time in which they do not exist. So the mystic's account does not answer their position. We must follow what we have established here, which, in this period of Islamic philosophy, we have been the first to prove fully. If earlier Muslim philosophers or scholars had reached this conclusion, it would have been well known, since they had every reason to investigate it.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00512

The closest argument presented here is one attributed to an early Christian thinker: “The world has limited power, and whatever has limited power has a limited duration. So the world cannot have existed forever.” The author of The Book of Discussions objects that the world may be limited in its own power to last, while lasting without limit because its cause is eternal and continuously supplies unlimited effects and motions. I say that his reply is ambiguous and misleading. “It does not last forever by itself or by its own power” may mean that its possible essence does not, by itself, give it lasting existence, but that it lasts through existence from the Necessary Being. Perhaps that is not what the argument meant. The argument may instead be that the actual existence of these bodily substances has limited power, not merely that their essences do not give them endless power. Their essences do not exist at all apart from existence, so it makes no sense to say that their essences have unlimited power.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00513

The reply may also mean that their actual existence, which comes directly from the Maker, has only limited power, but keeps receiving new power and effects from its eternal cause. That can be understood in two ways. First, perhaps each particular bodily existence has only limited power and does not last forever, but it produces unlimited effects through the continuous help of the higher source. This is false: the existence of a body's features and effects depends on the body itself, and the substantial body is stronger in existence than anything that follows from it. Existence reaches those features only through the body on which they depend. If the effects and results are unlimited, the intermediate cause must also be unlimited, whether it is an immediate agent, a receptive power, a tool, or a subject.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00514

This is not disproved by prime matter, which can receive an unlimited number of effects. It can receive them only through an unlimited succession of preparations and powers. Its lasting unity is an indefinite unity that is renewed each moment as new forms and powers arise.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00515

The second interpretation is that, although the world's existence at each moment has only limited power, the first source gives its matter a new power and a new identity at every moment, different from the one it gave before. But this is exactly the view that the world comes to be and passes away: each individual in it is preceded by temporal nonexistence. That is the very position of the three revealed religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. One could object to the argument by saying that something in the world, such as separate intellects, has unlimited power. That would work only if those separate forms were part of the world in the sense relevant here. You will learn from our account that separate forms, precisely insofar as they are separate, are not part of what is other than God. So the claim that the world and everything in it has limited power and does not last forever as an individual remains sound. It lasts only as a general meaning, not as one individual reality.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00516
XXXVI. What the “Now” Is, and How It Exists and Passes Away
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00517

Know that “now” has two meanings. One depends on time; the other is what gives rise to time by flowing. In the first sense, the now is a boundary of continuous time. We must ask how it exists and how it ceases to exist. You know that time is a continuous quantity, and anything continuous can be divided without end in principle, though not in fact. Such division happens in one of three ways: by an actual cut, by a change in the aspect under consideration, or by the mind's imagination. An actual cut cannot be made in time, as you have seen. So time can be divided in either of the two remaining ways: motion may bring something to a point all at once, creating a shared boundary such as sunrise or sunset, or the mind may divide it through its power of imagination.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00518

To explain how the now ceases to exist, first recall a principle Avicenna teaches in The Healing and elsewhere: one thing's existence or nonexistence in time can be instantaneous or gradual. It is instantaneous when the thing comes to exist or ceases to exist all at once, in a single instant. If it continues to exist, that instant is the first instant of its existence. If it does not continue, as with things that exist only for an instant, that instant alone is where it occurs. Or a thing may exist gradually: it has one continuous existence that can unfold only across one continuous stretch of time that matches it. We call this gradual existence. It does not mean that many separate things occur in the parts of that time. In its own nature, the thing is one, though it can be divided in principle. Before we divide it, it is one thing extending across one stretch of time. It has no first endpoint at which it exists, since it cannot come to exist at just one end or boundary. It must exist together with the whole stretch of time. Once we divide it, its parts are found one after another in the corresponding parts of time. This kind of gradual existence has no first instant. It exists through time, not at its boundary. A third possibility is that something exists in time without being spread across it. It does not have a continuous existence that matches time part for part, but it exists during that time because there is no instant in it at which the thing is absent. It has no first instant of existence, either at the beginning of that time or within it. This way of setting out the issue clears up many doubts.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00519

One objection comes from the author of The Summary. He says that a thing's full existence or nonexistence must either come about little by little, across a stretch of time that matches it and can be divided along with it, or all at once, in a single instant that must be the first instant of its existence or nonexistence. He asks how there could be a third option: a thing that begins to exist but has no first instant. The answer is that these two options are not direct opposites. The opposite of “coming about little by little” is simply “not coming about little by little.” That includes both things that begin at a particular instant and things that do not.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00520

Likewise, the opposite of “beginning at a particular instant” is simply “not beginning at a particular instant.” That, too, includes both things that come about gradually and things that do not. So a third kind is possible: a thing exists throughout a stretch of time and at every part of it, but not by extending across it; and it does not exist at the start of that stretch. The argument and closer examination show that this middle case occurs when things begin to exist. The same applies when things cease to exist, in all three ways, as we will explain. To settle the categories, follow Avicenna's argument in The Healing: ask whether the shared instant between two stretches of time can contain one state in the first stretch and a different state in the second. A thing that can be in either of two opposite states cannot be in neither at that instant. Some things occur in an instant and have the same state at every instant in which they exist; they do not need to match a stretch of time. Examples include contact, squareness, and other stable shapes. Such a thing is present at the shared instant.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00521

Other things exist only in the second stretch of time; the instant between the two cannot contain them. Motion is one example: its state does not stay the same from instant to instant. At each instant, it brings a new degree of closeness to the goal and distance from the starting point. It begins only after the shared instant, throughout the following stretch of time and all its instants. The same is true of things that come about only through motion, such as the absence of contact that follows contact. These things have no first instant of existence. Otherwise, either the new instant would directly follow the shared instant, so that two instants touched, or a stretch of time would lie between them. In the second case, the thing would be neither moving nor at rest, or neither in contact nor out of contact, during that stretch. In short, motion through the middle of a path certainly exists.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00522

The motion of passage cannot exist at the instant that marks the end of one stretch of time, because that is the last instant of rest. That instant also lies at the end or beginning of the path, so the moving thing cannot be halfway between the path's start and end there. After that instant, however, motion exists at every instant and in every part of the time it occupies. No second instant can follow the first directly, since that would make the instants touch. So motion exists throughout a stretch of time and at every instant in it, but has no first instant of existence. The same holds for anything whose existence depends on motion but does not require a fixed amount of motion. It also holds for things that exist only in an instant, such as a particular kind of contact between two cones: the contact occurs at an instant, but its absence has no first instant.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00523

Once you understand these points, we can ask how the now itself ceases to exist. The now, or anything else that exists only in an instant, cannot cease gradually, because that would divide it and make it last through time. If it ceases all at once, either its instant of nonexistence is the same as its instant of existence, which would make two instants touch, or it comes later. If it comes later, there must either be a stretch of time between the two instants, during which the now continues to exist, or no stretch between them, which again makes two instants touch. Both are impossible. So the now ceases to exist throughout all the time that follows it. This is a third kind of change, and it is a real one.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00524

You might say: even if the now is absent throughout all the time that follows, we are asking when its absence begins. Surely that beginning does not occupy the whole following stretch of time. So it must happen either gradually or all at once, and the same problem returns. We reply that “beginning” has two meanings. It can mean the boundary of the time in which something occurs; or it can mean the first instant in which the thing occurs. In the first sense, the absence of the now begins with the now's own existence. In the second sense, its absence has no beginning. As we have seen, not every changing thing must have a first instant in which its change is already under way. Motion has no first instant of motion, and rest has no first instant of rest.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00525

The first kind—things that occur all at once—includes all things that happen in an instant, such as reaching a point on a path, arriving at the goal of motion, becoming square or hexagonal, taking on other shapes, making contact, and one circle or line meeting another. Each has a first instant and continues to exist for a time. The second kind—things that exist gradually—includes motion across a path, the amounts of time, and all the states that depend on motion and do not remain fixed, such as sounds. The third kind includes motion through the middle of a path; things produced by motion, such as an angle formed as one line moves alongside another; a gap that opens between two surfaces or lines; separation after contact; the absence of arrival or contact; and, in general, anything that can come about only through motion without its existence being divided into parts. It also includes the nonexistence of things that occur in an instant, when they cease after the last instant of their existence, and many other cases. These are all cases in which the now that depends on time exists as time's boundary, formed in one of the two ways we have described.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00526

The other meaning of now is the flowing now that produces continuous time as it flows. To understand it, notice that distance, motion, and time match one another in every respect that concerns their existence. Just as we can imagine a point that, by moving, traces out a distance, so there is something in motion—the moving thing's being between the start and end of its path—that, by flowing, produces motion across the whole path. If so, time must also have something flowing that produces time as it flows. This is called the flowing now. It matches motion through the middle of the path. The point that draws a line is not the same as the points that mark its ends; likewise, motion through the middle is not the same as instant arrivals or other events that happen all at once. The source of time is also different from an instant we imagine within it. The flowing now is time's source because it produces time through its motion and flow. Take this to heart.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00527
XXXVII. How Motion and Its Effects Can Cease to Exist
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00528

There is a problem about how motion across a path, and the time that matches it, cease to exist. Some say that motion and its corresponding time are absent at all times other than the stretch in which they exist. In other words, motion exists only during one stretch of time and is absent at all other times. But this does not answer our question. We are asking how motion passes away—how it begins to be absent after it has existed.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00529

There is a second problem. Existence and nonexistence are opposites: a thing cannot be neither or both at once. If something exists gradually, little by little, then as each part of it comes to be, the absence of that part ends. The existence of this part does not end the absence of some later part; that absence remains until the later part exists. A gradual thing's existence and nonexistence therefore both unfold little by little. So if a thing exists gradually, its absence should also be gradual. This seems to create a problem. We need to look more closely.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00530

First, understand that motion and time have a weak kind of existence, mixed with nonexistence. The same is true of something that changes gradually over time, such as a color that deepens or an amount that grows. Its existence over time is weak and mixed with nonexistence. Just as it exists gradually, so it is absent gradually. Its time of existence is also its time of nonexistence.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00531

Motion, however, can be considered in two ways. First, we can consider it as the gradual change of something else from what it could be into what it is. Here we are looking at that thing's category and its gradual existence. Second, we can consider motion in itself and ask what kind of existence motion has. These are different questions. In the second sense, motion does not exist gradually, and so its absence does not have to be gradual either. In this respect, motion exists all at once: its nature is the gradual change of something else, but it is not itself a gradual change. Motion within motion would be impossible, as we have explained. Time is similar. It measures something's gradual existence, but it is not a measure of its own nature.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00532

So motion and time, and things like them, each have two kinds of existence and two kinds of nonexistence. One kind is the existence or nonexistence of a thing that unfolds gradually. The other is the existence or nonexistence of the gradual process itself, or of a thing considered together with its gradual nature. The first is gradual; the second is all at once. In this sense, motion exists in the mind. This also explains why someone may say that becoming something and ceasing to be it happen all at once, while someone else may say that they happen gradually. Neither is wrong: each is speaking about a different aspect.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00533

Avicenna says in a passage of this kind that there is no first instant in which something is moving, at rest, coming to be, or passing away, because time can always be divided further. The author of The Summary objects: there is no first instant in which something is moving or at rest, but there is a first instant in which something comes to be or passes away, since its form appears or disappears all at once. Avicenna's wording, he says, is therefore not right.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00534

I reply that coming to be is indeed instantaneous, as the author of The Summary reports from Avicenna. But there is no proof that Avicenna says the same of passing away. And anyone who says that forms come to be all at once must also say that they pass away in a way that has no first instant. Our view, however, is that both coming to be and passing away happen gradually. Otherwise matter would be left without a form. When water becomes air, the airy form cannot appear while the water form is still present; nor can it appear in the last instant of the water form. It must appear in a different instant. Then either two instants touch, which is impossible, or matter is left without either form. Avicenna may have pointed toward the truth here: his words suggest that both forms come to be in a stretch of time that can be divided endlessly.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00535
XXXVIII. How the Instant Measures Time
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00536

For geometers, a measure is a part of a length or number that can be taken away again and again until nothing remains. The instant does not measure time in this sense. But “measure” can also mean something that makes a thing ready to be counted in the first sense. The instant measures time in this second sense: it gives time unity, and repetition gives it plurality. As you know, time is continuous. We can count it only after dividing it, and division requires boundaries. Once boundaries are set, continuous time is split into parts, which can then be counted by one of their own parts. A line, for example, is divided by points. A point makes it possible to count the line's parts, while those parts themselves measure the line in the first sense. So the instant and the parts of time measure time in different ways.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00537

One writer says that the instant both separates and joins time. It separates the past from the future, but it also joins them because it is their shared boundary. The instant is one thing in itself, but it can be considered in two ways: as the end of the past and as the beginning of the future. As a joining point, it is one in itself and in the way we consider it, because it is the shared point between the two.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00538
XXXIX. How Motion Divides Time, and Time Measures Motion
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00539

We have already seen that the continuity of a path, as a path along which motion occurs, causes time to exist. Motion through each part of the path causes the corresponding part of time to exist. So motion is a measure of time in the sense that it makes time's earlier and later parts exist. Time, in turn, measures motion by counting it, since time determines the amount of motion. Think of people and numbers: ten people make the number ten exist, while the number ten makes it possible to count them as ten. Ten is ten in itself; people are counted as ten by means of it.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00540

The same is true of time and things that exist in time, such as motion. Time's existence is its amount, and motion causes it to exist—not because motion causes time to be an amount, since being an amount is part of what time is. Time measures motion in two ways. It makes motion have a certain size, and it tells us how much motion there is. Motion measures time by showing how much earlier and later there is in it. There are also two ways to show an amount: a measuring cup can show how much liquid it contains, and the liquid can show how large the cup is. A path can show the amount of motion, as when we say “a journey of two miles”; motion can show the length of a path, as when we say “the distance of a throw.” But only one of these gives a measure in itself: it is continuous by its nature, so we call it long or short; and because it can be counted through what comes before and after, we call it great or small in number.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00541
1. Eastern Insight
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00542

Distance, motion, and time exist as one thing. They do not exist as three separate things that happen to be connected; the mind separates them and assigns each a different role. Distance is an individual instance of length, size, or another category. Motion is its renewal, its gradual passage from what it could be into what it is. That renewal is an idea the mind draws from the thing. The continuity of motion is the continuity of the path itself, and time gives that continuity a measure and a definite amount. After separating these aspects in thought, we may say that one causes another. The path's continuity gives motion its continuity—but this does not mean that one continuity causes a second, separate continuity. Motion's continuity is the path's continuity considered as motion.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00543

Someone might imagine motion that is not continuous, as those who believe in indivisible parts do. But time's continuity is not caused in the same way. Time is, by its nature, a continuous quantity. Its existence still needs a cause, and that cause is not the continuity of the path by itself; it is the path's continuity as carried through motion.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00544
XL. What Exists in Time
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00545

Avicenna says in The Healing and elsewhere that something exists in time only if it has an earlier and a later state. These belong directly to motion, and to a moving thing indirectly. He also says that kinds and parts of a thing are in it; the instant is in time as unity is in number; earlier and later are in time as even and odd are in number; hours and days are in time as two and three are in number; motion is in time as the ten categories are in the number ten; and a moving thing is in time as the subject of those categories is in the number ten. Rest is the absence of motion. It is not measured by time in itself, but because it is bounded by two motions, it gains a kind of earlier and later, so we imagine it as existing in time.
The fourth kind: Power that produces different actions with awareness
passage-en-00546

I say that every substance has some kind of change, or is affected by change. We have already shown that nature itself is renewed. So anything at rest in one respect is moving in another, and in that respect it exists in time in itself. In our account, time follows the ongoing renewal of nature as a whole. It then follows the circular motion, which is the oldest of the motions, especially the motion of the outermost sphere. That motion measures other motions from place to place and changes of position; through those, it measures changes in quality and quantity. Changes in other categories—such as relation and possession, and even nonexistence and possibility—follow the change of substance and so are motions only indirectly. Their earlier and later order in time is indirect as well. Things that are neither motions nor involved in motion do not exist in time. Their coexistence with changing things is called timeless duration. Likewise, when changing things coexist with one another not as changing but as stable, that coexistence is timeless duration.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00547

I. Where Motion Begins and Ends, and When Its Endpoints Oppose Each Other
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00549

The starting point and destination may also be opposites, or nearly so. In quality, motion from black to white joins true opposites. Motion from yellow to indigo joins things that are like opposites: one is closer to white, the other to black. In quantity, motion from an object's larger natural size to its smaller size joins the two extremes. Growth and shrinking that do not reach either extreme lie between opposites. Places, by themselves, are alike, but they can be opposed by direction. Natural motion from the highest place to the lowest is from one opposite to another, since these are the only two natural directions. If natural motion takes place between them, its endpoints are like opposites.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00550

For motion that is not natural, its endpoints are opposed in two ways. First, places are like parts of a size: two of them cannot occupy the same point. Second, the starting point and the destination are opposed as beginning and end. In this way, the endpoints become opposites indirectly. In circular motion, however, the beginning and end are not a single point, as some suppose. Motion is continuous, and each part of it has a beginning and an end that cannot occur together. In a body's change of position, any position can be treated as a beginning or an end, since the body cannot occupy the two positions at the same time. So what serves as a beginning or an end may exist only as a possibility, or it may exist in fact.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00551

The beginning and end, and their relation to motion, are alike in this respect. Each is related to the motion as a relative term is related to its counterpart: a beginning is the beginning of what begins, and an end is the end of what ends. But they are not necessarily related to each other: understanding a beginning does not always mean understanding its end. A motion could have no beginning or no end, as with the motions of the people of Paradise. Since both beginning and end are positive realities, their opposition is not a matter of presence versus absence, or of a thing and its lack. The only kind of opposition left is contrariety. You may ask: how can opposites exist in one body, when opposites cannot be together?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00552
We reply that opposites can exist together in a subject that is not their immediate subject. The immediate subjects of beginning and end are not the body itself, but its positions and states.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00553
II. Why Motion Does Not Occur in the Other Five Categories
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00554

We have already given a brief account of this. Here is a fuller explanation. Relation has no independent nature; it depends on something else. If that underlying thing moves, rests, grows, shrinks, strengthens, or weakens, the relation follows its change. It changes through that thing, not by itself.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00555

As for “when”—the time at which something exists—Avicenna says in The Deliverance that time exists for a body through motion. So how could time itself have motion? Every motion occurs in time. If time itself moved, there would have to be another time in which it moved. In The Healing, Avicenna says that moving from one year to another, or one month to another, seems to happen all at once. I have already explained how a gradual process can be considered as a whole and so exist all at once. Many later thinkers found Avicenna's words troubling and objected to them. I addressed their objections in my commentary on The Guidance. Avicenna also says that “when” may be like relation: there is no motion in it; instead, motion occurs first in quality or quantity, and time changes or remains steady as a result.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00556

But time depends on a changing category in a different way from relation. Time is not a separate, momentary feature of that category. Motion is the category's own renewal, not something that merely follows it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00557

The same is true of “when” and “having.” Some say motion occurs in the categories of acting and being acted upon. That is wrong unless they mean that one and the same motion can be viewed from the side of the mover or from the side of what is moved. If they mean a separate motion in those categories, their claim does not hold. When something changes from cooling to heating, either the cooling continues, which would mean that one thing is moving toward opposites at once, or it ends before the heating begins. In the second case, there must be a pause between them. So there is no single, continuous motion from cooling to heating.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00558

I can state the point more briefly. Motion in a category means that the category comes about little by little, so that it has a different instance at each instant of the motion. Anything that cannot exist in an instant cannot have motion in it. Otherwise the instant would have to last through time.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00559
Someone may object that a thing can gradually lose its ability to act—not because the thing it acts on becomes less able to receive the effect, but because the agent's own condition changes.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00560

We reply that if the action is natural, the agent's power may weaken little by little; if it acts by choice, its resolve may fade; and if it acts through a tool, the tool may wear out. In every case, the power, resolve, or tool changes first. The agent's ability to act changes as a result, not in itself. So this objection does not apply.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00561
III. What Rest Is, What Kind of Rest Opposes Motion, and How a Body Can Have Neither
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00562

When a body is not moving, there are two possible meanings. It may continue to exist in one place, size, quality, or other state. Or it may lack a motion that it is able to undergo. People have agreed to call only the second meaning “rest,” the absence of motion. They give two arguments for this choice.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00563

First, rest is agreed to be the opposite of motion. Opposites must have definitions that are themselves opposed. Motion has been defined as the first completion of something that is able to change, in so far as it is able to change. So the definition of rest must oppose some part of this definition. If rest were a positive state, it would still have to be a kind of completion, since every positive existence is a completion. It would then have to be either a second completion of what is able to change, or a first completion of what is already actual. The first option would mean that every rest must be preceded by motion; the second, that every rest must be followed by motion. Both claims are false. So rest must oppose completion and be something absent: the lack of motion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00564

If we instead define rest first as a positive state—being in a place—we would have to add that the thing remains there. We could say it stays in the same place for a stretch of time, or for more than an instant, or that it is in the same place before and after. But we know what a stretch of time is only through motion, and we have assumed that motion can be understood only through rest. That would be circular, which is impossible. So motion must be defined first, and rest defined in a way that opposes it. This works only if rest is the absence of motion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00565

The second argument is that each kind of motion has something absent that opposes it. Growth is opposed by a halt in growth; change in quality by rest; motion from place to place by the absence of such motion. The rest that opposes growth is not a continuing size, but the absence of change in size. The rest that opposes change in quality is not a continuing quality, but the absence of that change. The same is true of rest that opposes motion from place to place, or any other motion. This is not just a dispute about words, as some have claimed. Some say that the rest opposed to motion is rest at the starting point; others say it is rest at the destination. Each side has arguments. The truth is that rest in a place opposes both motion away from that place and motion toward it. Rest is not the absence of one particular motion, since then every motion would count as rest in some other direction. It is the absence of any possible motion in that category.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00566

If we insist that natural motion must be opposed by natural rest, then natural upward motion is opposed by rest in the upward direction, since that is the natural direction—not by rest below. Downward natural motion is opposed by rest at the lower destination. So the rest that opposes motion is at its destination. As for how a body can be free of both motion and rest, there are three cases.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00567

The first is a body that cannot leave its natural place, such as the heavenly spheres or the elements considered as a whole. These bodies do not move from their places, but they are not at rest either. Rest is the absence of motion in something that can move. If a body cannot move, it cannot be at rest in this sense. It is fixed in its place, neither at rest nor in motion. The second case is a body that is not touched by the same surrounding surface for more than an instant, such as a fish in flowing water or a bird in moving air. It is not moving, because its position does not change in relation to things outside it. But it is not at rest, since it does not remain in one place for a stretch of time, as rest requires.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00568

The third case is any instant in the time of a motion, including its beginning and end. A body is neither at rest nor in motion at that instant, because motion can be divided without limit and cannot occur in an instant. If a body cannot be called moving in an instant, it cannot be called resting in an instant either.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00569

I say that each of these three cases needs closer examination. For the first, some define the possibility involved in rest by the nearest kind of motion. On that view, the elements as a whole can be called at rest in place, even though they do not move. The second case assumes that a place is the surface that surrounds a body. But we can say that the fish and bird are at rest in their place even if those surrounding surfaces change: the change does not come from them, as with a passenger on a moving ship. Motion requires an agent that acts and something able to be affected. If no agent moves an existing thing, there is only rest.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00570

As for the third case, the body is described as moving throughout every instant of the time of its motion, but not as moving within the instant itself. You may say: if motion does not exist in the instant, the body is not moving then, so it must be at rest, the opposite of motion. We reply that the opposite of “motion within a single instant” is merely “no motion within that instant,” not “no motion at all.” The body need not be at rest simply because it does not complete a movement inside a single instant. It is described as moving during the stretch of time that the instant bounds. Yes, in each instant of its motion the body is without motion in that instant, and also without rest in that instant. These are not true opposites, because time is part of the definition of each. Lacking a specific kind of motion does not mean lacking motion altogether.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00571
IV. How One Motion Can Be One Event, One Kind, or Another
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00572

You know that motion is a positive state of its subject, and that it depends on six things. Its unity depends on some of them. The unity of one particular motion requires the unity of its subject and its time. A shade of white in one body is not the shade of white in another. And if a body's whiteness returns after it has disappeared, the returning whiteness is not the same one that disappeared. Just as the subject's being one kind or another does not by itself make whiteness a different kind, it does not by itself make motion a different kind. A kind is different only when its essential features differ. Other categories are features of the subject; they do not define its kind. Many different categories can therefore exist in one subject. One particular motion is the one whose subject, time, and path are the same.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00573

If any of these differs, the motion is different as an individual, though not necessarily as a kind. Motion differs in kind when its defining starting point, path, or destination differs. For example, motion from a beginning to an end along a straight path differs in kind from motion along a circle. Motion from black to white differs in kind from motion from black to green and then indigo. Rising and falling differ in kind. So it is wrong to say that blackening and whitening follow the same path and differ only in their starting and ending points, or that rising and falling differ only by incidental features. Straight and circular motions differ in kind because their paths differ in kind. Circular motions with different degrees of curvature also differ in kind, as do motions through black and through white, because the quality in which they occur differs. Motions that belong to the same kind are not opposites. Speed and slowness do not change a motion's kind. Motion in quality and motion in quantity differ in their general kind.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00574

Some people doubt that motion can be one thing, since it is always passing away and being renewed. We have already answered this. Motion, considered as motion, cannot be divided into two separate motions. In that sense it is one, just as the number ten is one in itself, even though it counts ten things. Motion also exists in the world, whether we understand it as motion across a path or as the moving thing's being between the path's start and end.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00575

Some have answered the objection by comparing motion to a house or a living thing. These can keep the same form even as parts are removed and replaced: a brick is taken from a house, a new one fills the gap, and the house remains. But motion and number are not like a house or a living thing. In each of those, form and matter together make the thing one; their unity includes a possible or actual multiplicity. That is not true of motion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00576

Bahmanyār writes in At-Tahsil that he is not persuaded by such answers. A changing thing cannot have one lasting form unless its parts remain unchanged from the moment it begins to exist until it passes away, all joined to one fixed form or power that preserves it by replacing its parts. A house with a missing brick is not the same as it was before the loss: its arrangement is a feature that ends when its supporting parts change. Nor is a shadow on flowing water the same shadow from one instant to the next, because it depends on the water. When the water changes, the shadow does not remain.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00577

I say that the unity of motion is not like the unity of a house or anything like it. It is more truly one. The unity of the subject in growth and decline has already been explained. In their view, the circular motion of the heavens, considered as the moving thing's being between past and future, remains one forever. In our view, it changes at every instant. Yet the changing material forms of each heavenly body have one lasting intelligible form, which remains through God and stands between its earlier and later changing forms. That is the link between the changing and the unchanging. Motion across a path, by contrast, seems to be one only in an indirect sense. Its unity is not like the unity of motion through the middle of the path, which is a single, intelligible whole; motion across a path can be divided in principle.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00578
V. What Speed and Slowness Are, and Why They Are Not Caused by Pauses
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00579

Motion cannot be indivisible, or divided into parts that cannot be divided further, even in principle. So speed and slowness cannot be caused by pauses within motion. First, if motion could not be divided, neither could the path it covers. But the path can be divided without limit, as we will show when we discuss bodies. Motion matches the path, and the path is continuous because the body is continuous. A body can be divided without limit, so motion can be divided without limit too.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00580

Second, suppose one motion were faster and another slower because pauses occurred within the slower one. Then the slower moving thing would sometimes appear to be at rest, and a spinning wheel would seem to break into separate parts. The time taken by the faster motion is to the time taken by the slower motion as the distance covered by the slower motion is to the distance covered by the faster one. If two moving things start and stop at the same times, and one motion lasts one tenth as long as the other while the distances they cover differ by thousands, the slower one should appear to stop during parts of its time when it is not moving. Its continuous motion would be broken into sections. This is not what we see in examples such as the sun's motion and a horse running at full speed. Other clear arguments support the same conclusion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00581
VI. Further Points About Speed and Slowness
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00582

Speed and slowness have the same basic meaning in straight and circular motion, and in changes of size and quality: covering a distance in less time. In natural motion, resistance from the medium can make movement slower. In forced motion, a thing's own nature resists the movement. In motion by choice, both kinds of resistance may play a part. Speed and slowness are not opposites in the way that two relative terms depend on each other. Nor are they simply presence and absence. If two motions take the same time, the faster one covers more distance. If they cover the same distance, the slower one takes more time. Each has something the other lacks, so neither is simply the absence of the other. Their difference must therefore be a difference between opposing qualities.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00583

If speed and slowness are opposing qualities that admit greater and lesser degrees, each should have an extreme: a greatest speed and a greatest slowness. How can there be a motion with no faster motion, or one with no slower motion? The power that produces motion has a limit, so it sets a limit to speed. The limit to slowness comes from resistance to motion, such as resistance from the medium or from a thing's own nature when it is forced to move. Al-Tusi raised a related problem in a letter. If speed and slowness are needed to distinguish one particular motion from another, and each can be defined only by time, then time helps make a particular motion what it is. How, then, can one particular motion be the cause of time? We cannot say that motion in general causes time while each particular motion is made particular by time, because only a particular motion causes time. How can this problem be resolved?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00584

I know of no one who has answered this. The answer that occurs to me is that time belongs to motion only when we examine the two in thought. As explained earlier, motion and time exist together as one reality. Time does not attach to motion as an outside feature attaches to a thing. It is more like a feature that belongs to what a thing is, as a kind belongs to a broader kind or existence belongs to what exists. Such features can be earlier in one sense and later in another. A particular motion in the world is shaped by a particular time; in thought, that time is a feature of motion considered simply as motion. In that sense, time can be called the cause of the particular motion, and motion the cause of its time. This is true when we analyze them in thought. In the world itself, there is no separate cause and effect, or feature and subject: motion and time are one thing.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00585
VII. When Motions Oppose Each Other
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00586

Motions of different kinds are not opposites. A single subject can undergo change in quality, growth, and movement from place to place. If these changes conflict at some moment, the conflict comes from outside causes, not from what those kinds of motion are. Motions within the same kind can be opposites: becoming black and becoming white, or growing and shrinking. Each is directed toward a natural limit. The opposition between two motions must involve one of the six things on which motion depends. It is not due to the subject: things with opposite natures can move in the same way, as fire rises naturally while water can be forced upward. It is not due to time, which has no opposite. Nor is it due to the path, since the same path can be traveled in opposite directions. The agent does not explain the opposition either.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00587

So the opposition must come from where a motion begins and where it ends. When those points are opposed, the motions are opposed. A motion from black toward clear is not the opposite of a motion toward black, because its destination is not white. Opposed motions are those whose starting points and destinations face each other, either because the qualities themselves are opposites, as black and white are, or because one motion begins where the other ends. A motion is not related to its starting point and destination only by accident. Its nature includes both leaving one point and aiming toward another. So these points help make the motion what it is, even though they do not make its subject what it is.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00588
VIII. Why Straight and Circular Motions Are Not Opposites
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00589

Straight and circular motions are not opposites. Straightness and curvature are not two states that replace each other in the same thing while it remains the same. A line cannot change from straight to curved without ceasing to be that line. Straightness and curvature are either features that define a line or features belonging to different kinds of line. In either case, changing one into the other means the line itself has changed. The same applies to circular paths with different curves: they do not replace one another in the same subject.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00590

You already know that motions are not opposites just because their paths differ. If a circular motion were opposite to a different motion because of its starting and ending points, then a straight motion could match its endpoints in reverse: what the straight motion begins from would be what the circular motion ends at, and the two would run in opposite directions. There could also be endlessly many circular arcs and matching straight chords, which would give one motion endlessly many possible opposites. But one motion cannot have many opposites. Nor would those arcs all be the same kind of path; they would differ in kind, not just in individual case.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00591

Still, things that are not opposites in themselves can oppose each other in another respect. In character, for example, the middle ground is opposed to both excess and deficiency. Excess and deficiency are opposites in themselves, because both are faults; the middle ground is opposed to them because it is a virtue. So the middle is a middle in one respect and an extreme in another. Some say that circular motions in opposite directions are not opposites because they do not have different endpoints. Every pair of opposite motions, they say, must have different endpoints. There is room to examine this claim.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00592

You have seen how straight motions can oppose each other. Rising and falling oppose each other as straight motions, and also because one goes upward and the other downward. A motion has an opposite when it covers the shortest path from one actual endpoint to another, and the opposite motion goes from that endpoint back to the first—not somewhere else. So motion in the order of the zodiac is not opposite to motion against that order. Nor is motion along one half of a circle opposite to motion along the other half. A circle has no one arc that is singled out from the others. For each point, moving toward it is the same as moving away from it; each point is both the goal and the point to leave.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00593
IX. Why Every Straight Motion Ends in Rest
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00594

Earlier philosophers gave four arguments that a period of rest must come between any two different motions. The first goes like this: a thing can touch a point and then be separate from it only at two different instants. There must be time between those instants, since one instant cannot follow another without a gap. There is no motion during that time, so the thing must be at rest. We can answer, first, that this argument could be applied to every point along the path. That would mean no continuous motion could exist. Second, separation is itself a motion and must take time. Its final instant has no motion in it; it is the instant when touching ends. There is no problem with contact holding at the boundary of the time when separation begins.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00595

The second argument says that if upward motion joined directly to downward motion, the two would form one continuous motion. Then two opposite motions would be one, which is impossible. The reply is that a line with an actual shared endpoint is not one line, especially when its two parts go in different directions, like the sides of an angle. For two lines to form one continuous line, their shared endpoint must exist only as a possibility, not as an actual point. The same applies to motion. An actual shared boundary does not make two motions one. The third argument says that if rising flowed straight into falling, the end of the upward motion would lead back to the place below it. Then the thing it was moving away from would become its goal. The reply is the same: this would follow only if the two motions had to be one, with no actual boundary between them.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00596

The fourth argument is similar. If becoming black changed directly into becoming white, with no time between, then the power to become black would also be the power to become white. A white thing would then have the power to become white, and a black thing the power to become black. But nothing can be in the process of becoming what it already is. The reply is that a thing does not begin becoming black while it is still white. Blackening starts from blackness and comes after whiteness; the thing's later motion toward white does not begin while it is still white. So the argument does not show that one and the same power must produce both changes.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00597

These inherited arguments are weak. Avicenna's proof is stronger. A body's driving tendency is the immediate cause of its movement from one point on a path to another. The force that moves the body must remain with it. So this tendency must still be there when the body arrives at a point. That is possible, since a tendency can begin in a single instant, unlike motion itself.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00598

When the body turns back from that point, a different tendency causes its return. One tendency cannot cause both arrival at a point and turning away from it. The new tendency begins at an instant, but not the instant when the first one has just brought the body to its destination: one body cannot have opposing tendencies at the same instant. So there must be time between the two tendencies, when the body is at rest.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00599

These points are sound, but we must understand “turning away” in the proof as turning back from a destination, not simply leaving any point along the path. Otherwise the proof would fail at each point the body passes. The proof applies to opposite motions that need different driving tendencies, and two opposing tendencies cannot be in one body at one instant.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00600

Al-Fakhr objected that this proof does not work for changes in size or quality, because they do not need such a tendency. I say this is mostly a dispute about the word. We can replace “driving tendency” with whatever immediate cause has the same role: it must differ when the result differs. Another objection uses a ball fixed to a turning wheel, with a flat surface above it. As the ball rises, it touches the surface at one instant in every turn, neither before nor after. The reply given to this is poor, so I will not spend time repeating it or explaining its weakness. I will answer this puzzle when I discuss the example of a seed thrown upward.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00601

Those who deny that there is rest between motions offer a stronger argument. Suppose a stone stops between rising and falling. Its nature still acts on it. If the force pushing it upward is stronger than its nature, it should keep rising. If weaker, it should already be falling. If they are equal, the stone should remain at rest.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00602

We reply that the unusual force given to the stone should not disappear by itself. If it has a cause, perhaps it is the resistance of the air, which weakens that force. But air resists only while the stone is moving, not while it is still. So that force should remain, and the stone should not fall again unless something pushes it. If it does remain at rest, the rest cannot be natural, because the stone's nature is being held back. It would have to be forced rest. That would mean the outside force gave the body a special power to keep it at rest for a time, as Avicenna claims. But this cannot be right for two reasons. The outside force might give the stone an added power without giving it a power to rest; if it gave both, opposite powers would remain together, which is impossible.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00603

Second, when the outside force first gave the stone this added power, it was not a power to rest. It later became one. If nature stopped it from acting, then nature was no longer stopping it once the forced power had overcome nature. If both powers were equal, why was a separate power to rest needed at all? Their balance should remain, and the stone should not fall. It is also strange that Avicenna says elsewhere that, without the air's resistance, a thrown stone would reach the outermost sphere, yet here he says the outside force gives it a power to rest at certain places. The two claims are hard to reconcile.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00604

I say that nature itself causes this rest, once the outside force has weakened. The force weakens because nature resists it and because the air's impacts prepare the way. Those impacts happen just before the body reaches the place where it stops. We can see the forced power weaken as the air pushes against it. These impacts prepare the conditions for rest; nature is the direct cause. This is what Avicenna means when he says the outside force gives a body a power to rest in certain places: the power that moved the stone upward becomes, when balanced by nature, part of what keeps it still. It remains so until the stone's own nature overcomes it and moves the stone downward.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00605

The Imam's answer is that rest must occur at the end of a motion, because at the last moment a body can no longer be described as moving. Rest is therefore necessary and needs no cause, just as other necessary features need none. On this view, the stone need not stay above: once the necessity ends, its nature moves it. This answer is weak in several ways. First, rest is an absence that still needs a cause. Even if rest means being in one place, size, or quality for a time, or follows from such a state, that state has a positive cause. It is not enough to say that the cause of motion is absent. Second, if the necessity of rest can end, something must cause it to end.
